summaryEn: It makes the wiring that connects things — but sells it as engineering rather than as parts, spread across industrial, green energy, automotive, medical and communications customers. Dividends have compounded from NT$2.75 to NT$10 in a decade; two of its five end markets are currently shrinking.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; solutions framing — the 76.95/23.05 assembly-versus-component split, the five-way end-market diversification, 19.31% ROE and a decade of compounding dividends credited, but FY2025 EPS falling to NT$13.02 from NT$14.70, green energy −14.19% and communications −12.99% in 2026Q1, a 4.16× price-to-book, and 2026Q2 operating cash flow of −NT$58m against NT$910m of net profit all stated plainly; sector 電子工業 → Connectors & Cable Assemblies)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Sinbon Electronics (信邦電子, TWSE: 3023) makes **the wiring that connects things** — cable assemblies, wire harnesses and connectors. Founded in **1989** and **listed in August 2002**, it sits in a category that sounds like the definition of a commodity, and has spent three decades proving otherwise by selling **engineered solutions designed for a specific customer's product** rather than catalogue parts from a shelf.

The distinction shows in the revenue split. As of March 2026, **cable and connector assemblies were 76.95% of revenue and connectors and components 23.05%** — meaning most of what Sinbon sells is a **complete assembly** it designed, not an individual part. A wire harness for a medical imaging system, a solar inverter or an industrial robot must be specified, validated and manufactured to that product's exact requirements, and once designed in, it stays for the product's life. That produces gross margins around **24–25%** and, more importantly, customer relationships measured in product generations.

The other defining feature is **deliberate diversification**. Sinbon's end markets, by March 2026 revenue, were **industrial 33.08%, green energy 21.06%, communications and electronic peripherals 19.30%, automotive 16.95%, and medical and healthcare 9.61%** — five genuinely unrelated demand cycles. Very few companies in this collection are spread this evenly, and the design is intentional: no single downturn can take out the business.

**It is also being tested right now.** In 2026Q1, **medical grew 18.02% and automotive 21.04%, industrial 10.63% — while green energy fell 14.19% and communications and electronic peripherals fell 12.99%**. Two of five markets are contracting and three are growing, which is precisely what diversification is supposed to look like in practice. Group revenue for January–May rose **7.01% to NT$14.29bn**, and monthly revenue has accelerated to **+18%**.

The financial record is strong but not unblemished. Annual EPS ran **NT$12.21 (FY2022) → 13.73 → 14.70 (FY2024) → NT$13.02 (FY2025)** — a decline last year — with **2026 first-half EPS of NT$7.36** ahead of the prior year. **Trailing return on equity is 19.31%.** Dividends have compounded remarkably: from **NT$2.75 (FY2014) to NT$10.25 (FY2024)** and **NT$10.0 (FY2025)**, a **3.55% yield** at NT$281.50 on a roughly **77% payout**.

Two cautions. The shares trade at **21.1× earnings and 4.16× book** — a quality multiple that assumes the compounding continues. And **2026Q2 operating cash flow was −NT$58m against NT$910m of net profit** — a single quarter, explicable by working capital in a growing business, but a gap worth watching. The honest read: **a genuinely differentiated engineering business with exceptional diversification and a decade of compounding dividends — priced accordingly, with two end markets currently going backwards.**

Sinbon was founded in **1989**, making connectors and cables. On paper this is among the least differentiated products in electronics: a connector joins two things, a cable carries a signal, and thousands of companies make both. Competing on price in that market is a route to permanently thin margins.

Sinbon chose a different position: **sell the design, not the part**. Rather than offering a catalogue of standard connectors, it works with a customer's engineers to specify a complete **cable assembly or wire harness** for a particular product — the right conductors, shielding, connectors, moulding, routing and terminations, validated to that product's electrical, mechanical and regulatory requirements. The customer receives a working sub-assembly rather than a box of components to integrate themselves.

Two consequences follow, and they define the company. First, **margins are engineering margins rather than component margins** — gross margin runs around **24–25%**, and **assemblies are 76.95% of revenue** against **23.05% for standalone connectors and components**. Second, and more valuable, **the position is sticky**: once an assembly is designed into a medical scanner or an industrial robot, replacing it means redesign, revalidation and often regulatory requalification. Customers do not switch to save a few percent.

The third decision was **where to sell it**. Sinbon deliberately spread across unrelated industries rather than concentrating where growth looked fastest. Today the mix is **industrial 33.08%, green energy 21.06%, communications and electronic peripherals 19.30%, automotive 16.95%, and medical and healthcare 9.61%**. These cycles are genuinely independent — solar installation, factory automation, vehicle production, hospital equipment purchasing and network build-out do not move together.

The payoff has been consistency. **Dividends have risen almost every year from NT$2.75 in FY2014 to NT$10.25 in FY2024** — a compounding record almost no Taiwanese electronics company can match, and one built not on a single winning product but on a business model that keeps working across several industries at once.

- **1989 (6 Dec)** — Sinbon Electronics founded, making connectors and cables.
- **1990s–2000s** — Shifts from selling components to designing **customised cable assemblies and wire harnesses**, positioning as a solutions provider rather than a parts supplier.
- **2002 (26 Aug)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (3023)**.
- **2010s** — Deliberately diversifies across **industrial, green energy, automotive, medical and communications** end markets. Dividends rise from **NT$2.75 (FY2014)** through **NT$4.0 (FY2017)** to **NT$6.29 (FY2020)**.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$12.21**; dividend **NT$8.46**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$13.73**; dividend **NT$9.6**.
- **2024** — Peak of the recent record: **FY2024 EPS NT$14.70**; dividend **NT$10.25**.
- **2025** — A softer year: **FY2025 EPS NT$13.02**, with quarterly EPS of **3.85, 3.16, 3.05, 2.96**; dividend **NT$10.0**.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$3.60**, up 21.79% on the prior quarter. End-market growth splits: **medical +18.02%, automotive +21.04%, industrial +10.63%**, but **green energy −14.19%** and **communications and electronic peripherals −12.99%**. March revenue of **NT$2.906bn** is a record for the month.
- **2026Q2** — **EPS NT$3.76**, first-half total **NT$7.36**; **ROE 19.31%**; monthly revenue growth accelerates to **+18%**. **Operating cash flow of −NT$58m against NT$910m of net profit.**

Sinbon's accounts show **a consistently profitable engineering business with a remarkable dividend record and one recent cash-flow gap**.

- **Earnings that grew, dipped, and are recovering.** Annual EPS: **NT$12.21 (FY2022) → 13.73 (FY2023) → 14.70 (FY2024) → NT$13.02 (FY2025)**. The FY2025 decline was real — quarterly EPS fell through the year (**3.85, 3.16, 3.05, 2.96**) — and **2026's first half at NT$7.36** is ahead of the prior year's NT$7.01, with **2026Q2 EPS of NT$3.76** the best quarter in six.
- **Stable margins, which is the point.** Gross margin has held at **23.0–24.7%** across six quarters, with operating margin between **8.3% and 13.0%** and net margin **9.1–11.3%**. For a business selling wiring, that stability is the evidence that it is selling design rather than copper.
- **Return on equity of 19.31%** on **NT$16.53bn of equity** — high, and achieved without unusual leverage.
- **A dividend record that stands out in this collection.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$2.75 (2014) → 3.1 → 3.7 → 4.0 → 4.48 → 5.3 → 6.29 → 6.96 → 8.46 → 9.6 → NT$10.25 (2024) → NT$10.0 (2025)**. That is **almost fourfold in a decade**, with only one small step down. At NT$281.50 the **3.55% yield** sits on a payout of roughly **77%**.
- **The one thing to watch.** **2026Q2 operating cash flow was −NT$58m against NT$910m of net income.** A single quarter of negative operating cash flow in a growing business is usually working capital — receivables and inventory building ahead of shipments — but the size of the gap is notable and should converge in following quarters.
- **A moderately geared balance sheet.** **NT$35.08bn of assets** on **NT$16.53bn of equity** — a **52.9% debt ratio** — with **NT$6.80bn of cash**.
- **A quality valuation.** **21.1× earnings and 4.16× book.** That is a full price, justified only by the consistency of the returns and the dividend record; it leaves little room if the FY2025 dip repeats.

The financing reality: **a high-return, well-diversified engineering business with an outstanding distribution record — priced as a quality compounder, with one quarter's cash conversion to reconcile.**

**Stance: an engineering-led cable assembly business with genuine five-way end-market diversification, 19.31% ROE and dividends up almost fourfold in a decade — at 21x earnings and 4.16x book, with two of its five markets currently shrinking.**

The bull case:

1. **It sells design, not parts.** **Cable and connector assemblies are 76.95% of revenue**, engineered to a customer's specific product. Once designed into a medical scanner or an industrial system, the assembly stays for that product's life — replacing it means redesign and revalidation. That is why gross margin holds at **23–25%** in a category that ought to be a commodity.
2. **Diversification that actually works.** **Industrial 33.08%, green energy 21.06%, communications 19.30%, automotive 16.95%, medical 9.61%** — five independent cycles. **2026Q1 is the proof: medical +18.02%, automotive +21.04% and industrial +10.63% while green energy −14.19% and communications −12.99%**, and group revenue still grew **7.01%**.
3. **A compounding record.** Dividends from **NT$2.75 (FY2014) to NT$10.25 (FY2024)**, with **19.31% ROE** and stable margins throughout. Few Taiwanese electronics companies have this consistency.
4. **Momentum returning.** **2026Q2 EPS of NT$3.76** was the best in six quarters, monthly revenue is running **+18%**, and management guided Q2 ahead of Q1.

The counter-arguments:

- **FY2025 went backwards.** **NT$14.70 → NT$13.02**, with EPS declining every quarter through the year.
- **Two end markets are contracting.** Green energy — over a fifth of revenue — fell **14.19%**, and communications fell **12.99%**.
- **The valuation is full.** **21.1× earnings and 4.16× book** for a business growing revenue at single digits.
- **Cash conversion.** **2026Q2 operating cash flow of −NT$58m against NT$910m of net profit** needs to reverse.
- **The dividend eased.** **NT$10.25 → NT$10.0**, on a **77% payout** — comfortable, but no longer rising.

A **quality-compounder** thesis: a genuinely differentiated business bought at a quality price — where the diversification is the moat and the multiple is the risk.

Sinbon sells **engineered interconnection**, and the model rests on one distinction:

- **Assemblies, not components.** **76.95% of revenue is cable and connector assemblies** — complete wire harnesses and sub-assemblies designed for a specific customer product — against **23.05% for standalone connectors and components**. The customer receives something that works in their machine, not a bag of parts.
- **Why that is defensible.** Designing an assembly means specifying conductors, shielding, connectors, moulding, routing and terminations to meet a product's electrical, mechanical, environmental and regulatory requirements — then validating it. In **medical** applications that includes regulatory qualification; in **automotive**, durability and safety standards. Once designed in, changing supplier means **redesign, revalidation and requalification** — expensive relative to the part's cost, so customers do not switch casually.
- **The five end markets, and why the spread is deliberate.** **Industrial (33.08%)** — factory automation and machinery; **green energy (21.06%)** — solar, wind and EV charging infrastructure; **communications and electronic peripherals (19.30%)**; **automotive (16.95%)**; **medical and healthcare (9.61%)**. These cycles genuinely diverge, which is the whole point: **2026Q1 saw three grow and two contract simultaneously**, and group revenue still rose.
- **The economics.** Gross margin **23–25%**, operating margin **8–13%**. High-mix, lower-volume, engineering-intensive manufacturing carries more design and support cost than commodity production, which is why the operating margin is well below the gross — and why the position is defensible.
- **The financial shape.** **19.31% return on equity** on a **52.9% debt ratio**, with **NT$6.80bn of cash**, supporting a dividend that has risen from **NT$2.75 to NT$10** in a decade.

The levers are **design wins, end-market mix, engineering capacity and working capital**. The strength is that Sinbon's competitive position is created **at the design stage** rather than at the price negotiation, and is spread across industries that do not fall together. The vulnerability is that the same model requires **continuous engineering investment and working capital** — which is the likely explanation for **2026Q2's negative operating cash flow against NT$910m of profit**, and the thing to watch.

Interconnection is a large, fragmented industry that splits sharply between commodity and engineered work.

- **The commodity half.** Standard connectors and cables are made in enormous volume by suppliers worldwide and sold from catalogues on price and availability. Margins are thin, competition is global, and there is no defensible position.
- **The engineered half, where Sinbon operates.** **Custom cable assemblies and harnesses** designed for a specific customer product. The competitive assets are **application engineering, qualification experience and manufacturing flexibility for high-mix, lower-volume production** — not scale. Global competitors include **TE Connectivity, Amphenol and Molex** at the large end, with numerous regional specialists below them; Sinbon competes as a mid-sized specialist with a deliberately broad end-market spread.
- **Why the end markets matter more than the product.** Because the product is similar across industries, a company's fortunes are determined by **which industries it serves**. Concentrating in one — as many component makers do — imports that industry's cycle wholesale. **Sinbon's five-way spread is the strategy**, and **2026Q1 demonstrated it working**: green energy down 14.19% and communications down 12.99%, offset by medical up 18.02%, automotive up 21.04% and industrial up 10.63%.
- **The structural growth drivers.** **Electrification** raises interconnection content everywhere: an electric vehicle carries far more high-voltage wiring than a combustion one; solar and wind installations need extensive cabling; factory automation adds sensors and connections; medical devices grow more electronic each generation. The content-per-unit trend is favourable across all five markets.
- **The green energy caveat.** That segment — over a fifth of revenue — fell **14.19%** in 2026Q1, a reminder that renewable installation is **policy-driven and lumpy**, as **TSEC (6443)** elsewhere in this collection demonstrates far more dramatically.

Sinbon's position is **defensible at the design stage and diversified at the market level** — an unusual combination. The industry truth is that **in interconnection, the money is made by being specified in, not by being cheap** — and that a supplier's real risk is not competition but its customers' industries all turning at once.

**Strengths**
- **Engineered assemblies are 76.95% of revenue** — designed in, hard to displace without revalidation.
- **Genuine five-way diversification**: industrial **33.08%**, green energy **21.06%**, communications **19.30%**, automotive **16.95%**, medical **9.61%**.
- **19.31% ROE** with stable **23–25% gross margins**; **NT$6.80bn of cash**.
- **Dividends up almost fourfold in a decade**: **NT$2.75 (FY2014) → NT$10.25 (FY2024)**.

**Weaknesses**
- **FY2025 EPS fell to NT$13.02** from NT$14.70, declining every quarter through the year.
- **Green energy −14.19%** and **communications −12.99%** in 2026Q1.
- **2026Q2 operating cash flow −NT$58m** against **NT$910m** of net profit.
- **21.1× earnings and 4.16× book** — a full quality valuation.

**Opportunities**
- **Electrification** raising interconnection content across all five end markets.
- Medical (+18.02%) and automotive (+21.04%) growth continuing; **2026Q2 the best quarter in six**.
- Recovery in green energy and communications from a low base.

**Threats**
- Several end markets weakening simultaneously, defeating the diversification.
- Large global competitors (TE Connectivity, Amphenol, Molex) targeting the same engineered work.
- Working-capital demands as growth resumes.

- **The valuation assumes the compounding resumes.** **21.1× earnings and 4.16× book** for a company whose **FY2025 EPS fell from NT$14.70 to NT$13.02**, with revenue growing at single digits. Quality multiples are unforgiving when the quality pauses, and FY2025 was a pause.
- **Two of five end markets are contracting.** **Green energy — over a fifth of revenue — fell 14.19%** and **communications and electronic peripherals fell 12.99%** in 2026Q1. Diversification is working today because three others are growing; it stops working if the weakness broadens.
- **Cash conversion.** **2026Q2 operating cash flow of −NT$58m against NT$910m of net income** is the single specific number to monitor. In a growing engineering business this is usually receivables and inventory ahead of shipments, and it should reverse — but a persistent gap between profit and cash is always the more important signal.
- **Green energy is policy-driven.** Solar, wind and EV charging demand depends on subsidy regimes and installation timetables rather than on economics alone — the same exposure that produced far more severe outcomes at **TSEC (6443)** elsewhere in this collection.
- **Competition from scale players.** **TE Connectivity, Amphenol and Molex** have far greater resources and are equally capable of engineered assembly work when a programme is large enough to interest them.
- **The dividend has stopped rising.** **NT$10.25 (FY2024) → NT$10.0 (FY2025)** at a **77% payout**. It is comfortably covered, but the decade-long increase — a central part of the investment case — paused with the earnings.

Sinbon's outlook depends on **whether the growing end markets keep outrunning the shrinking ones.** The axes to watch:

- **Green energy and communications.** Down **14.19%** and **12.99%** in 2026Q1, together accounting for about **40% of revenue**. Stabilisation in either would materially change the group's growth rate; further decline would test whether three growing markets can carry two falling ones.
- **Medical and automotive momentum.** Growing **18.02%** and **21.04%** — the highest-value, most qualification-intensive segments, and the ones where design-in positions last longest. Continued growth here improves both the mix and the durability of the business.
- **Quarterly EPS against the FY2024 peak.** **NT$14.70 (FY2024) → NT$13.02 (FY2025)**, with **2026 first-half EPS of NT$7.36** and **2026Q2's NT$3.76 the best in six quarters**. A full year above NT$14.70 would confirm the dip was temporary.
- **Operating cash flow.** **−NT$58m against NT$910m of net profit in 2026Q2.** This should converge as shipments catch up with the working capital; if it does not, it becomes the story rather than a footnote.
- **The dividend.** **NT$10.0 for FY2025** after **NT$10.25**, at a **77% payout**. A resumed increase would signal management's confidence that FY2025 was the exception.

Bottom line: Sinbon turned one of electronics' most commoditised products into an engineering business — **76.95% of revenue in designed-in assemblies**, spread deliberately across **five independent end markets**, earning **19.31% on equity** with **stable 23–25% gross margins** and **dividends up almost fourfold in a decade**. It is also a company whose **FY2025 earnings fell**, whose **green energy and communications segments are contracting**, which trades at **4.16× book**, and which posted **negative operating cash flow against NT$910m of profit last quarter**. Judge it on **end-market breadth and cash conversion** — a genuinely differentiated compounder, bought at a compounder's price.
